examples.description: Trace this package's fixtures and gate the committed reports against them. Named `examples` rather than `callidescope` so every examples package in this workspace runs the same way, and so it is never confused with `codebase:callidescope`, which is its mirror image: that target only ever publishes, because a report there goes stale on nearly every change and depth is gated by each project's own inferred `gate` instead, while the fixtures traced here are frozen, so a stale report means a fixture, the resolver, or one of the three dependency packages this run's closure reaches moved — which is exactly the regression this package exists to catch. Those three packages' sources are named in `inputs` alongside the toolchain, because the closure measures them and their callables reach the committed reports, so a cached result is never replayed over a change to them. Their READMEs are not named, because this run publishes a `## 🔭 Callidescope` section only for the project it is scoped to. `{projectRoot}/examples/*/README.md` is named for the opposite reason: `gated-leaf` is a nested project this run is scoped to as well, so it carries that same section in its own guide, and `{projectRoot}/README.md` alone never reaches it — a hand-edit inside those anchors would otherwise replay a cached green over exactly the drift `--check reports` exists to catch. `{workspaceRoot}/configuration/*.config.ts` is named for a different reason and is not redundant with `shared-globals`, which holds `configuration/tsconfig.json` and nothing else: two of those three packages are in the closure only because this package's own `eslint.config.ts` and `codometer.config.ts` spread the root ones, and the root ones import `@codebase/logger/eslint` and `@codometer/configuration`. Drop an import there and the committed reports lose a whole project while every other input is untouched, so a cached green replays over exactly the drift `--check reports` exists to catch. The glob rather than those three files by name, because a closure is whatever the compiler read and a hand-written list of it goes stale in silence — which is the failure this input exists to prevent. It is a per-target input and never belongs in `shared-globals`, where a high-churn glob once cost the whole workspace every cache hit it had. Depth is not gated here at all: the deep fixtures are meant to breach, which is why `configuration/.callidescopeignore` keeps them out of the workspace run.

codometer.description: Measure one project and gate the limit it declares, writing the report the pull request's ⏲️ Codometer section reads. This default depends on `build` because size analysis reads compiled output; the workspace-root `codebase:codometer` target must NOT, because it measures source and waiting on every build would be both slow and circular — it pins `dependsOn` to an empty list of its own so this default can never reach it, and neither half of that asymmetry may be collapsed into the other. The command runs with `cwd` set to `{projectRoot}` rather than the workspace root: codometer has no `--directory` flag of its own and always measures the process's own working directory, so running there is what makes a project's `limits[]` address paths like `Compiled JavaScript.size` rather than ones synthesized under a `Command Line` input, and it is also what lets `--config`'s upward-ancestor search land on the project's own `codometer.config.ts` instead of the workspace one. `main.ts` is addressed with a literal `../../` rather than `{workspaceRoot}` for the same reason — the working directory it runs from is no longer the workspace root, and Nx only resolves the `{workspaceRoot}` token when it opens the whole option's value, not when it appears partway through one; this entry reaches every project that sits exactly two directories below the workspace root, which is every project except the ones nested under `packages/ic-suite/<suite>/`, whose own four-directories-deep override sits below. `SWC_NODE_PROJECT` is pinned the same way, to the shared base every project's own tsconfig already extends: `@swc-node/register`'s ESM hook resolves its tsconfig as `<cwd>/tsconfig.json` with no upward search, so a project with no `tsconfig.json` of its own — `affirmations`, which is pure Python — would otherwise fail to load `codometer-cli` at all rather than measure anything, the same way `codometer-cli`'s own `start` target already pins this for the same hook. `--output-json` is a bare flag rather than a path, so it writes wherever the resolved configuration's own `json` output says to — the shared configuration's `codometer-report.json`, the same path for every project — and a target that left the flag off would write nothing at all and still exit clean — contributing nothing to the ⏲️ Codometer section and looking exactly like a project that changed nothing — so passing it is what makes the report exist, not something the tool refuses to run without. `--output-markdown README.md` stays a literal path on the command line because only the `write` configuration passes it, which is what keeps a branch's `check` run from rewriting every project README; `check` adds `--check limits` so a breach fails only after the report is on disk. Neither checks staleness: project READMEs are written on main by the release workflow, so they are expected to be stale on a branch. The report this target writes is subtracted from its own inputs, because `production` would otherwise glob it back in and every run would rewrite the hash it was just cached under — a local run could never hit its own cache, and a fresh checkout could never match one. `README.md` stays an input despite also being an output: codometer measures markdown, so an edit to it genuinely changes the measurement, and restoring it from cache writes back the identical bytes.

lint-codebase.description: Static code analysis: every check that judges what the repository commits rather than what a build produces. Nearly all of them read the source without executing it; `meanderaw:meanderaw-check` is the one exception, booting that project's own container to regenerate the whole corpus and diff it against what is committed, because catching drift in a generic renderer or an enumerator needs the real pipeline run rather than a static read of its output. An nx:noop aggregator — the work is the dependsOn targets, which Nx schedules in one graph rather than spawning a process per tool. `codebase:codometer`, `codebase:callidescope`, and every synchronization command on the `synchronization` project are deliberately not among them: `codometer` and `callidescope` each publish a report on the default branch, and Nx forwards an explicit configuration down `dependsOn`, so listing one here would make `--configuration=write` publish that report from a branch. Each synchronization command is its own Nx target rather than a shared aggregate, for the same reason. What each one gates is named directly by whatever gates it instead: the inferred per-project `gate` target — which carries no configuration of its own, so there is nothing here for `dependsOn` to forward — and each derivation synchronization's own `:check` join this target in one `nx affected` invocation, in the Lint Codebase workflow and in `configuration/lint-staged.config.ts` alike, and the per-project `codometer` limits belong to Make Projects, which builds first. A pull request and a commit therefore still trace depth and check derivation drift — what this target alone no longer covers, the invocation around it does.

start.description: Run the Meanderaw application. With no arguments it sweeps every meander into output/meanders.sqlite — the whole lattice's unit space, enumerated and classified, then the historical corpus's hardcoded Codes beyond that budget; with --args="--rows <n> --columns <n> --code <code>" it writes that one row; with --args="--check" it regenerates that same sweep into a throwaway database and fails if it disagrees with the committed one, which `meanderaw-check` runs on every commit. `build` compiles this project rather than drawing anything, so populating the database is this target's job.

meanderaw-check.description: Regenerate the whole sweep — the generalized enumeration and the historical corpus's hardcoded ingestion, exactly what a real sweep runs — into a throwaway in-memory database, and diff it against the committed output/meanders.sqlite, failing on any new, missing, or changed row. This is what catches drift in the generic renderer, the enumerator, or a Characteristic's own logic before it reaches the committed corpus, the same CI role `address-table` once played for the retired per-family procedural pipeline. Deliberately uncached, for the same reason that target was: it reads the committed database rather than any declared build output, so caching it buys nothing while a stale hit could hide real drift — and the sweep itself costs under a minute, not the hours a cache exists to save. `--check` is a boolean flag rather than a `check`/`write` configuration pair, unlike `address-table`: nothing here can "fix" drift by rewriting the committed database from a branch, since that database is populated by a real `start` run a person chooses to make, not by an aggregator's own `--configuration=write`.

start.description: Runs every synchronization command in one process — the only target that does. conventional-config.description: Reconciles derived conventional-commit configuration against `configuration/conventional.config.cjs`. `check` runs on a pull request; `write` runs on the default branch's release.

devcontainer-configuration.description: Reconciles the cloud devcontainer configuration's synced fields against the local one. `check` runs on a pull request; `write` runs on the default branch's release.

issue-labels.description: Adds the type and scope labels a submitted `issue.yml` body implies. Its destination is GitHub itself rather than a file, so reaching it needs a token that neither a fork nor a developer's `lint-codebase` run has: the 👮 Audit Issues workflow runs it directly through node rather than through this Nx target on an issue's `opened` event, and nothing else names it. This target exists for a human running it locally with their own credentials.

pull-request-labels.description: Reconciles this repository's GitHub label vocabulary against `configuration/conventional.config.cjs`. The two are deliberately different and must not be collapsed into one. `options.env.SWC_NODE_PROJECT` is written out for the same reason: the `codometer` targetDefault points it at `../../configuration/tsconfig.json`, relative to a per-project run's own `{projectRoot}` cwd, and this target already overrides `cwd` back to `{workspaceRoot}` — merging the targetDefault's `env` in unchanged would resolve two directories above the repository entirely. `@swc-node/register`'s ESM hook needs this pointed at a real tsconfig to load `codometer-cli` at all, since it resolves `SWC_NODE_PROJECT` as `<cwd>/tsconfig.json` with no upward search. This is also the only run that reaches the workflows under .github, which belong to no project, so no per-project run ever measures them.

lint-codebase.description: Static code analysis: every check that judges what the repository commits rather than what a build produces. Nearly all of them read the source without executing it; `meanderaw:meanderaw-check` is the one exception, booting that project's own container to regenerate the whole corpus and diff it against what is committed, because catching drift in a generic renderer or an enumerator needs the real pipeline run rather than a static read of its output. An nx:noop aggregator — the work is the dependsOn targets, which Nx schedules in one graph rather than spawning a process per tool. `codebase:codometer`, `codebase:callidescope`, and every synchronization command on the `synchronization` project are deliberately not among them: `codometer` and `callidescope` each publish a report on the default branch, and Nx forwards an explicit configuration down `dependsOn`, so listing one here would make `--configuration=write` publish that report from a branch. Each synchronization command is its own Nx target rather than a shared aggregate, for the same reason. What each one gates is named directly by whatever gates it instead: the inferred per-project `gate` target — which carries no configuration of its own, so there is nothing here for `dependsOn` to forward — and each derivation synchronization's own `:check` join this target in one `nx affected` invocation, in the Lint Codebase workflow and in `configuration/lint-staged.config.ts` alike, and the per-project `codometer` limits belong to Make Projects, which builds first. A pull request and a commit therefore still trace depth and check derivation drift — what this target alone no longer covers, the invocation around it does.

make-projects.description: Measure the repository and gate the limits it declares over itself. An nx:noop aggregator, the way every project's `make-projects` is. `dependsOn` names `codometer` alone rather than inheriting the targetDefault's `build`: the root project builds nothing, and this run measures source. It exists so 👷 Make Projects reaches the repository itself — the workflows under .github belong to no project, so without this nothing gates their comment budgets.

scan-security.description: Security scanning: secrets, Python AST, dependency vulnerabilities, licenses, and infrastructure misconfiguration. An nx:noop aggregator.

callidescope.description: Publish the workspace call-stack trace: every project's README block, the mermaid diagram, and the JSON report. The only configuration left is `write` — depth checking now runs through the inferred per-project `gate` target, scoped by `nx affected` in the Lint Codebase workflow and `configuration/lint-staged.config.ts`, so a pull request and a commit gate the projects a change actually touched rather than the whole workspace. This target still stays out of `lint-codebase`'s `dependsOn` for the reason it always did, unchanged by that split because `write` is exactly the configuration that remains: Nx forwards an explicit configuration down `dependsOn`, so a target reachable from there would take `write` from `lint-codebase --configuration=write` and publish the report from a branch. `defaultConfiguration` is `write`, the only configuration left, so a bare `nx run codebase:callidescope` does what `:write` does. Publishing did not fan out the way gating did: one JSON report and one set of README blocks are what the whole workspace needs, and computing either per project would mean rebuilding the same call graph many times for one merged artifact, where gating benefits from being scoped to what changed and publishing does not. Four traced call-graph roots carry no gate of their own and never will, because a gate is inferred onto an Nx project and none of them is one. `configuration/` carries its own `tsconfig.json` and so is traced, measuring depth 3; three fixture roots under `packages/ic-suite/codependix/codependix-examples/examples/` are the same case at depth 0. All four keep being traced and published here on the default branch, so a regression in any of them still lands in the report; it only stops failing a pull request. The workspace root is a fifth gap of a different kind and is not one of the four: `configuration/.callidescopeignore` drops it as a project, for the reason recorded there, so the loose maintenance scripts it once owned are traced by nothing at all — which is also why the root project is skipped from gate inference, its scope being the workspace itself. The README glob is an input because `write` splices into those files: without it, a hand-edited report replays a cached run.

check-catalog-manifests.description: Enforce catalog: protocol for external dependencies in workspace package manifests

check-lockfile.description: Verify that pnpm-lock.yaml is in sync with package.json files

check-readme-projects.description: Verify the root README links to every workspace project

codependix.description: Export every configured Nx, NestJS, and file-import dependency graph, and gate the rules those graphs are judged against. Two configurations and no third, mirroring `codebase:callidescope` and `codebase:codometer`: this target is absent from `lint-codebase`'s `dependsOn`, so no run of it ever forwards a configuration here, and `write` means publish on the default branch and nowhere else. `check` runs `--check boundaries`, which reads no destination and writes nothing — a broken boundary is caused by the branch and fixed by it, so it gates every pull request, exactly where the inferred per-project `gate` target checks call-stack depth. The command line also accepts `--check reports`, which is what a bare `--check` used to mean, and nothing runs it: a configured export moves with the workspace it describes and would fail every branch that changed a project graph rather than anything the branch itself did. The release workflow runs `write`, after `callidescope` and the module-graph synchronization have run, so a project's `## 🕸️ Codependix` anchor reflects the same commit those write. The README glob is an input because `write` splices Markdown into anchor blocks placed by hand in those files.

commit-msg.description: Run the commit-msg git hook script (commitlint). Pass the commit message file via --edit=<path>.

commitlint.description: Validate commit message format with commitlint. The commit-msg hook calls the binary directly to avoid a project graph build; this target is for manual use.

conformetry-generate.description: Run the conformetry generate command from the workspace root

options.command: pnpm exec nx run conformetry-cli:start -- generate {args}

eslint.description: Lint workspace root files with ESLint — config files, scripts, documentation, infrastructure, and every markdown file in the workspace. That trailing `**/*.md` is what gives `project-structure/folder-structure` reach over markdown paths, and it is a workspace-wide glob rather than a list of directories on purpose: an enumerated list only judges the directories somebody remembered to add, so it would not have caught openwiki/ — the undeclared directory that motivated the rule — and would not catch the next one. Markdown inside a project is judged twice, here and by that project's own eslint target, which costs a second and reports the same answer.

fallow.description: Run all fallow static analyses (dead-code, duplicates, health) in advisory mode

fallow-audit.description: Fallow audit gate (new-only regression check on changed code) — advisory

fallow-dead-code.description: Fallow dead-code analysis (unused files, exports, types, dependencies, unresolved imports) — a `lint-codebase` gate beside `knip`, whose findings it deliberately mirrors: `configuration/fallow.config.jsonc` carries the same entry points, the same per-file report suppressions, and the same ignored dependencies as `configuration/knip.config.ts`, so a finding one reports the other reports too. The severities `knip` also fails on are `error` in that config; the rest stay `warn` and belong to `fallow-health` and `fallow-duplicates`, which are still advisory. The `write` configuration is identical to `check` because there is nothing to write: removing what this finds is `fallow-fix`, which stays manual-only.

fallow-duplicates.description: Fallow strict duplication analysis (config-driven) with threshold gating

fallow-fix.description: ⚠️  MANUAL-ONLY (write config): removes unused exports/deps from source files — never include in automated pipelines. Use check config for safe dry-run preview.

fallow-health.description: Fallow code health analysis (complexity, hotspots, maintainability) — advisory

gitleaks.description: Detect hardcoded secrets in git history using Gitleaks (detection only). The ci-incremental configuration scopes the scan to NX_BASE..NX_HEAD instead of full history, for push/pull_request/merge_group events where the weekly ci scan already covers everything older.

install-skills.description: Restore the skills listed in skills-lock.json from their source repositories into the gitignored .agents/skills/<name>/ folders. Also runs from postinstall; the force configuration re-restores skills that are already present.

jscpd.description: Run jscpd duplicate-code reporting and threshold status in advisory mode (never fails CI).

check.command: jscpd --config configuration/jscpd.config.json --no-tips --reporters console,threshold applications packages tools scripts configuration infrastructure || true

knip.description: Check for unused files, dependencies, and exports in workspace root only

lint-staged.description: Run lint-staged on staged files (invoked by the pre-commit git hook)

markdown-lint.description: Lint markdown files in workspace root (agents, scripts, documentation, infrastructure). Reaches .agents/ so this repository's own skills are linted like any other documentation; the vendored skills in skills-lock.json are excluded per skill in the markdownlint configuration. The inputs enumerate exactly the globs the command lints, plus the markdownlint configuration and shared-globals — the latter carries pnpm-lock.yaml, so a markdownlint upgrade cannot replay a cached pass. The workspace-wide default input is deliberately absent: it resolves to {projectRoot}/**/* for the root project, which made every root-owned file the tool never reads invalidate this cache. The vendored-skills negations then drop the 59 skills markdownlint already ignores, so editing one of them no longer busts the cache for nothing.

openwiki.description: Update OpenWiki content from code using the OpenWiki CLI (prints changes).

openwiki-update.description: Update OpenWiki content from code using the OpenWiki CLI (prints changes).

oxfmt.description: Format workspace root files with oxfmt (config files, scripts, documentation, infrastructure)

oxlint.description: Run Oxlint on workspace root files — config files, scripts, documentation, infrastructure, and the devcontainer sync scripts. That last path is named because the others hold no TypeScript at all today: `scripts/` went shell-only when the two dead root scripts were deleted, and oxlint exits non-zero when its paths match nothing, so a target covering only empty directories fails rather than passing vacuously. The devcontainer scripts are real TypeScript that nothing else here was linting.

pnpm-audit.description: Scan for fixable security vulnerabilities (check, which passes when the advisory registry is unreachable) or clean stale overrides and re-fix (write)

write.command: jq 'del(.pnpm.overrides)' package.json > package.temporary.json && mv package.temporary.json package.json && pnpm update --no-frozen-lockfile && pnpm audit --fix --ignore-unfixable; pnpm install --no-frozen-lockfile

postgres-container.description: Start, stop, or recreate the local PostgreSQL container (recreate removes the volume)

recreate.command: docker compose -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml down -v postgres && docker compose -f infrastructure/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d postgres

postgres-data.description: Dump and restore PostgreSQL data (databases, schemas, tables)

dump-dictionary.command: PGPASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres} pg_dump -h ${POSTGRES_HOST:-localhost} -p ${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432} -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres} -t forms -t inflections -t lexemes -t principal_parts -t pronunciations -t translations -t words -t word_forms -t word_lexemes -Fc -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-postgres} -f data/dictionary.dump

dump-literature.command: PGPASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres} pg_dump -h ${POSTGRES_HOST:-localhost} -p ${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432} -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres} -t authors -t lines -t texts -t tokens -Fc -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-postgres} -f data/literature.dump

restore-dictionary.command: PGPASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres} pg_restore -h ${POSTGRES_HOST:-localhost} -p ${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432} -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres} -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-postgres} -c -1 -t forms -t inflections -t lexemes -t principal_parts -t pronunciations -t translations -t words -t word_forms -t word_lexemes data/dictionary.dump

restore-literature.command: PGPASSWORD=${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:-postgres} pg_restore -h ${POSTGRES_HOST:-localhost} -p ${POSTGRES_PORT:-5432} -U ${POSTGRES_USER:-postgres} -d ${POSTGRES_DB:-postgres} -c -1 -t authors -t lines -t texts -t tokens data/literature.dump

pre-commit.description: Run the pre-commit git hook script (unstage notepads, lint-staged).

pre-push.description: Run the pre-push git hook script (branch name validation).

prettier.description: Format workspace root files with Prettier (excluding NX projects)

sherif.description: Lint codebase for consistent package.json conventions

write.command: pnpm dlx sherif@1.10.0 -p applications/JimmyPaolini --fix && nx run codebase:oxfmt:write

spell-check.description: Check spelling in every workspace root file no project owns (configuration, documentation, infrastructure, notepads, openwiki, planning, scripts, and the .agents, .devcontainer, .github, and .vscode directories). Reaches .agents/ so this repository's own skills are spell-checked like any other documentation; the vendored skills in skills-lock.json are excluded per skill in the cspell configuration. The inputs enumerate exactly the globs the command checks, plus the cspell configuration and dictionaries and shared-globals — the latter carries pnpm-lock.yaml, so a cspell upgrade cannot replay a cached pass. The workspace-wide default input is deliberately absent: it resolves to {projectRoot}/**/* for the root project, which made every root-owned file the tool never reads invalidate this cache. The vendored-skills negations then drop the 59 skills cspell already ignores, so editing one of them no longer busts the cache for nothing.

sync-vscode-settings.description: Validate that VS Code Machine settings contain all workspace settings (check) or merge workspace settings into Machine settings (write)

syncpack.description: Check dependency version consistency across packages (check) or fix mismatches (write)

write.command: pnpm exec syncpack fix --config configuration/syncpack.config.cjs && nx run codebase:oxfmt:write

trivy-config.description: Scan Terraform infrastructure code for misconfigurations using Trivy. Identical to what the Scan Security workflow runs, so a local run reproduces CI exactly. Requires trivy on PATH (the devcontainer installs it; otherwise `brew install trivy`).

options.command: trivy config infrastructure/terraform --format table --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 --ignorefile configuration/trivyignore

type-coverage.description: Check TypeScript type coverage for workspace root (minimum 95%)

validate-branch-name.description: Validate the current branch name against the configured naming convention. The pre-push hook calls the binary directly to avoid a project graph build; this target is for manual use.

vulture.description: Check root-level Python utilities for dead code

yaml-lint.description: Lint the workspace-root YAML no project reaches: the GitHub Actions workflows, composite action, and issue templates, the devcontainer and infrastructure compose files, the Helm chart and its values, the shared cspell and yamllint configuration, and the pnpm workspace file. The generated pnpm-lock.yaml is left out on purpose, and the Helm templates are skipped by the `**/templates/` ignore in yamllint.yaml because their Go template directives are not valid YAML. The installed skills under .agents/ are owned upstream and stay out. pyproject.toml and uv.lock are inputs because they pin yamllint itself: without them, a yamllint upgrade replays a cached pass and stops linting. Defined here rather than in the nx.json targetDefaults entry, which is filtered to language tags this project does not carry.

options.command: uv run yamllint -c configuration/yamllint.yaml .devcontainer .github configuration/cspell.config.yaml configuration/yamllint.yaml infrastructure pnpm-workspace.yaml
